claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a well-defined hierarchical heterostructure.
The considered HfNbTiVAl10 samples have minimal extrinsic defects.
The hierarchical architecture includes grain boundaries, phase boundaries, and substructural features.
These hierarchical interfaces mediate local stress distribution.
A machine-learning surrogate supplied with high-resolution structural descriptors can capture local load-transfer mechanisms.
A machine-learning surrogate supplied with high-resolution structural descriptors can capture fracture-initiation mechanisms.
Local load transfer and fracture initiation are typically resolved only by computationally intensive simulations.
Encoding high-resolution structural descriptors reduces model-error propagation.
Using the surrogate significantly lowers computational overhead.
The surrogate will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture properties with approximately 20% lower error than established simulations.
The surrogate will reduce computation time by at least a factor of ten relative to established simulations.
Finite-element and full-scale simulation methods are the established baseline for predicting mechanical performance in similar high-entropy alloys.
Sample-to-sample degradation or variability of the hierarchical heterostructure may cause the approach to fail.
Unexpected defect distributions may cause the approach to fail.
Environmental conditions absent from the training data, including extreme temperatures, may cause the approach to fail.
The achieved accuracy improvement and speedup depend on microstructural-data quality and training-sample representativeness.
Calibration across multiple sample sets will be necessary to refine the claimed accuracy and speedup values.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis jointly requires both the accuracy gain and the tenfold speedup, so failure of either requirement would falsify the conjunction. The declared rule instead requires both requirements to fail before rejection, allowing the hypothesis to survive when one of its two central predictions fails.
